text: Lesson 29 designed Meridian Health Partners' zero trust architecture across identity, segmentation, containment, and data controls. This lesson turns that design into something fundable: an honest maturity scorecard against the CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model, and a phased rollout roadmap sequenced the way a real budget cycle can actually absorb.

Step one scores each of the five CISA pillars against what's deployed today, not what Lesson 29 designed on paper. Identity and Devices sit at Initial, Networks and Applications & Workloads sit at Traditional -- a flat network and a legacy EHR with no gateway -- and Data stays at Initial even in the target column, because Lesson 29 classified patient data but hasn't yet built the enforcement that acts on that classification everywhere it lives.

Step two is refusing to average those five scores into one blended percentage. A single number hides that Data is Meridian's real risk and lets a committee fund whatever pillar is easiest to improve instead of whatever cuts the most actual risk. Five separate pillar scores, reported every time, keep that risk visible.

Step three sequences the rollout by risk reduction per unit of effort, the principle Chapter 7 already taught. Identity and Networks come first because they're mostly configuration against existing licensing. Data enforcement waits until phase three because it genuinely touches every system holding patient data, not one gateway in front of one legacy system. Vendor access review becomes a recurring phase four, not a one-time project.

Step four writes each phase as a one-pager a budget committee can act on: what changes, why it matters in plain language, what drives the cost, and what the risk is if the phase gets delayed. A line like 'one compromised clinic workstation can currently reach every patient record' gets budget approved faster than any amount of Conditional Access terminology.

Meridian now has a scored baseline and a sequenced roadmap -- the design looks genuinely strong on paper. Lesson 31's case study shows what happened when a very similar-looking rollout passed its own audit, and still got breached, through a gap the checklist itself never asked about.
